metadata.name: UX_UI_Heuristic_Evaluation_Quality_Framework
metadata.purpose: Provide a consistent standard for planning, running, scoring and reporting UX/UI heuristic evaluations across future projects.
source_basis: Nielsen Norman Group severity rating guidance
WCAG 2.2 accessibility principles and success criteria
Practical UX/UI review workflows for product teams

definition.what_it_is: A structured expert review where evaluators inspect an interface against agreed usability principles, identify problems, explain why they matter, and recommend improvements.
what_it_is_not: A replacement for usability testing with real users
definition.good_evaluation_outcome: The team can clearly see what is causing friction, who it affects, how serious it is, and what should be improved first.

quality_principles.principle: Evaluate against user goals, not personal taste
quality_principles.description: Every issue should explain how the interface affects a user trying to complete a task.
quality_principles.good_example: Users may not realise the consent request has been sent because there is no clear status change after sending.
quality_principles.poor_example: I do not like this button style.

quality_principles.description: Use the same core heuristic set across projects so findings are comparable over time.
quality_principles.good_example: Each finding is mapped to one primary heuristic and optional secondary heuristics.
quality_principles.poor_example: Each evaluator invents their own categories.

quality_principles.description: Record what was observed before jumping to a solution.
quality_principles.good_example: Observed issue: Error message says 'Invalid input' without naming the field. Recommendation: Show the specific field and how to fix it.
quality_principles.poor_example: Change the error message because it feels bad.

quality_principles.description: Severity should be based on impact, frequency, persistence, confidence and business/user risk, not loudness in a meeting.
quality_principles.good_example: Critical because it blocks users from submitting required evidence and affects compliance deadlines.
quality_principles.poor_example: Critical because a stakeholder mentioned it.

quality_principles.description: Findings should be written so a designer, developer or product manager can act on them without decoding UX fog.
quality_principles.good_example: The empty state does not tell users what to do next, so they may think the page is broken.
quality_principles.poor_example: The page lacks affordance salience within the interaction paradigm.

quality_principles.principle: Include accessibility as a core lens
quality_principles.description: Accessibility should be checked as part of the evaluation, not bolted on later like a wobbly roof rack.
quality_principles.good_example: Check keyboard access, focus order, contrast, labels, touch targets, error identification and screen reader meaning.
quality_principles.poor_example: Accessibility will be reviewed after launch.

quality_principles.description: Each issue should link to a screen, flow, screenshot, prototype frame, task or URL where possible.
quality_principles.good_example: Finding includes screen name, task, screenshot reference and affected component.

quality_principles.description: The best heuristic findings explain why the issue matters for user trust, speed, confidence, comprehension or task completion.
quality_principles.good_example: This reduces trust because the user is asked to confirm without seeing the consequence of the action.

core_heuristics.name: Visibility of system status
core_heuristics.plain_english: The interface should keep users informed about what is happening.
evaluation_questions: Does the system show progress, loading, saving, success and failure states?
Can users tell whether their action worked?
Are long-running actions explained clearly?
Are status labels meaningful and current?
evidence_examples: After selecting 'Send request', the status remains unchanged for several seconds.
The user receives no confirmation that the file has uploaded.

severity_triggers.low: Feedback is slightly delayed but the user can continue safely.
severity_triggers.medium: The user may repeat actions or hesitate because feedback is unclear.
severity_triggers.high: The user may submit duplicate data, abandon the task or lose confidence.
severity_triggers.critical: The user cannot tell whether a legally, financially or operationally important action has completed.

core_heuristics.name: Match between system and the real world
core_heuristics.plain_english: The interface should use language and concepts that make sense to users.
evaluation_questions: Does the language match what users actually call these things?
Are technical terms explained or avoided?
Does the flow match the real-world process?
Are dates, units, statuses and labels understandable?
look_for: Labels that mean different things to different users
evidence_examples: The label 'Denied' could mean the bill payer denied consent or an admin rejected the evidence.
The page uses internal product codes where users expect asset names.

severity_triggers.low: The term is mildly unclear but users can infer the meaning.
severity_triggers.medium: Users may need support or training to understand the interface.
severity_triggers.high: Users may make the wrong choice because the wording is ambiguous.
severity_triggers.critical: Ambiguous language could lead to compliance, consent, safety or financial mistakes.

core_heuristics.name: User control and freedom
core_heuristics.plain_english: Users should be able to undo, cancel, go back or recover from unwanted actions.
evaluation_questions: Can users cancel before committing?
Can users undo or reverse safe actions?
Are destructive actions clearly confirmed?
Can users leave a flow without losing work unexpectedly?
evidence_examples: Closing the drawer clears all unsaved selections without warning.
Deleting an uploaded proof has no confirmation or recovery path.

severity_triggers.low: Minor inconvenience with an easy recovery.
severity_triggers.medium: Users may lose small amounts of effort.
severity_triggers.high: Users may lose important work or need support to recover.
severity_triggers.critical: Users can accidentally cause irreversible legal, financial, safety or data-loss consequences.

core_heuristics.name: Consistency and standards
core_heuristics.plain_english: Similar things should look and behave in similar ways.
evaluation_questions: Are components used consistently?
Do similar actions use the same labels?
Do patterns match platform and product standards?
Are icons, colours and statuses used consistently?
look_for: Different components for the same job
Icons with unclear or changing meaning
evidence_examples: The same primary action is called 'Submit' on one page and 'Send' on another.
Warning colours are used for both errors and informational tips.

severity_triggers.low: Small inconsistency that does not affect task completion.
severity_triggers.medium: Users may slow down or second-guess the interface.
severity_triggers.high: Users may misunderstand actions or statuses across pages.
severity_triggers.critical: Inconsistency could cause serious mistakes in high-risk flows.

core_heuristics.name: Error prevention
core_heuristics.plain_english: The interface should prevent mistakes before they happen.
evaluation_questions: Does the design stop users from entering invalid data?
Are risky actions guarded?
Are required fields and constraints shown before submission?
Are defaults safe and helpful?
evidence_examples: The form only reveals that the tenancy end date is required after the user tries to submit.
Users can send a request without reviewing the selected meters.

severity_triggers.low: Mistake is unlikely and easy to fix.
severity_triggers.high: Mistake creates rework, support requests or incorrect records.
severity_triggers.critical: Mistake could cause compliance issues, data exposure, payment errors or safety risks.

core_heuristics.name: Recognition rather than recall
core_heuristics.plain_english: Users should not have to remember information from elsewhere.
evaluation_questions: Is key information visible when users need it?
Are choices explained in context?
Do users have to remember values from previous screens?
Are labels and summaries available before confirmation?
look_for: Users forced to copy information between pages
evidence_examples: The confirmation screen does not show which assets are included.
The table hides selected filters, so users cannot easily understand the current results.

severity_triggers.medium: Users may have to navigate back and forth.
severity_triggers.high: Users may make incorrect selections due to missing context.
severity_triggers.critical: Missing context could lead to serious approval, data or consent mistakes.

core_heuristics.name: Flexibility and efficiency of use
core_heuristics.plain_english: The interface should support both new and experienced users.
evaluation_questions: Can frequent users complete common tasks quickly?
Are bulk actions, shortcuts or saved settings available where useful?
Does the interface avoid unnecessary repeated work?
Can users filter, search, sort and scan efficiently?
evidence_examples: Users must open each meter individually to check consent status.
There is no way to filter by expired consent.

severity_triggers.low: Small efficiency issue for occasional users.
severity_triggers.high: Core workflows become slow at scale.
severity_triggers.critical: The product becomes impractical for large portfolios, high-volume tasks or urgent operations.

core_heuristics.name: Aesthetic and minimalist design
core_heuristics.plain_english: The interface should focus attention on what matters.
evaluation_questions: Is the most important information easy to find?
Is unnecessary content competing for attention?
Does the layout support scanning?
Are visual hierarchy, spacing and grouping clear?
look_for: Important warnings buried in the page
evidence_examples: The dashboard warning takes premium space but does not explain the next action.
Three secondary actions visually compete with the main task.

severity_triggers.low: Visual noise but task remains clear.
severity_triggers.medium: Users may take longer to understand the page.
severity_triggers.high: Users may miss important information or actions.
severity_triggers.critical: Critical information is hidden or visually deprioritised in a high-risk flow.

core_heuristics.name: Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors
core_heuristics.plain_english: Error messages should clearly explain what happened and how to fix it.
evaluation_questions: Does the error identify the problem?
Does it tell users how to fix it?
Is the error near the relevant field or action?
Does it avoid blame and scary system language?
look_for: Errors shown far from the problem
evidence_examples: The error says 'Failed' but does not explain whether the file type, size or connection caused it.
The form summary says there are errors but does not link to the fields.

severity_triggers.low: Error is slightly unclear but recovery is obvious.
severity_triggers.medium: Users may need trial and error to recover.
severity_triggers.high: Users may abandon the task or contact support.
severity_triggers.critical: Users cannot recover from a blocking error in a critical flow.

core_heuristics.name: Help and documentation
core_heuristics.plain_english: Help should be available when users need it, especially for complex or rare tasks.
evaluation_questions: Is guidance available for unfamiliar tasks?
Is help contextual rather than hidden in a giant manual swamp?
Are examples, tooltips or explanations provided where needed?
Can users understand consequences before acting?
look_for: Help hidden away from the task
evidence_examples: Users are asked to upload evidence but are not told what counts as valid evidence.
The CRREM page shows high-risk assets but does not explain how to interpret stranding year.

severity_triggers.low: Help would improve confidence but is not essential.
severity_triggers.medium: Users may need training or support.
severity_triggers.high: Users may complete the task incorrectly without guidance.
severity_triggers.critical: Missing guidance could cause legal, compliance, financial or safety issues.

additional_lenses.name: Accessibility and inclusive design
additional_lenses.mapped_to: WCAG 2.2 principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust
evaluation_questions: Can the interface be used with a keyboard?
Is focus order logical and visible?
Do text and meaningful UI elements have sufficient contrast?
Are form fields programmatically labelled?
Are errors announced and explained clearly?
Are touch targets large enough?
Does the interface avoid relying only on colour?
Can content reflow and zoom without breaking?
Are animations safe, purposeful and controllable?
common_findings: Focus state missing or too subtle
Form errors not linked to fields

additional_lenses.name: Content clarity
evaluation_questions: Is the copy written in plain language?
Does the copy explain what users need to know before acting?
Are labels specific enough?
Are instructions short, timely and useful?
Are empty states helpful?
common_findings: Long paragraphs where a short instruction would work
Empty state does not guide the next step

additional_lenses.name: Trust, consent and data confidence
evaluation_questions: Does the interface clearly explain what data is being used and why?
Can users see who gave consent, when and for how long?
Are privacy or data actions clear and auditable?
Does the interface avoid making uncertain data look certain?
Are confidence scores, assumptions or gaps explained?
common_findings: Users cannot see expiry or ownership details
System implies certainty where data is incomplete

additional_lenses.name: Responsive and cross-device behaviour
evaluation_questions: Does the layout work on common desktop, tablet and mobile sizes?
Are tables usable on smaller screens?
Do controls remain reachable?
Are important actions hidden or pushed too far down?
Does content reflow without becoming a tiny puzzle box?
common_findings: Primary action disappears below the fold
Modals too large on small screens

additional_lenses.name: Performance perception
evaluation_questions: Does the interface communicate loading states?
Are skeletons, progress indicators or optimistic updates used appropriately?
Can users continue working while data loads where safe?
Does slow loading create confusion or repeated actions?

recommended_evaluator_count.ideal: 3 to 5 evaluators when the project is high impact or complex
recommended_evaluator_count.reason: Multiple evaluators reduce blind spots and make findings less dependent on one person’s taste.

stages.description: Define what is being evaluated and why.
activities: Define product area, screen, flow or prototype scope
Define target users and their main goals
Define key tasks to inspect
Define known constraints, such as release deadline, technical limits or compliance needs
Confirm which heuristics and additional lenses will be used
Collect links to prototype, live environment, screenshots, analytics or support notes
Walk through each task from the user’s point of view
Record issues without discussing them with other evaluators
Capture screenshots or frame references
Map each issue to a primary heuristic
Add initial severity and confidence

stages.description: Evaluators compare findings and remove duplicates.
activities: Merge duplicate issues
Challenge vague findings
Agree primary heuristic
Agree severity rating
Check whether findings are evidence-based
Separate usability issues from bugs, content gaps and product questions

stages.description: Rank issues by user impact, risk and effort.
activities: Identify blockers first
Group related issues by journey or component
Highlight quick wins separately from strategic fixes
Use severity, frequency, affected users and confidence to prioritise
Call out issues that need user testing before solutioning

stages.description: Create a report that is clear enough to act on.
activities: Summarise the biggest themes
Show issue, evidence, impact and recommendation
Include screenshots where useful
State what was out of scope
Add next steps for design, product, engineering and research

stages.description: Make sure the evaluation leads to better design, not a dusty PDF goblin.
activities: Turn high-priority issues into backlog items
Review fixes against the original issue
Retest critical flows
Record what changed
Add reusable patterns to the design system if relevant

template.title: Short plain-English summary of the problem
template.screen_or_flow: Name of screen, flow, page, component or prototype frame
template.user_task: What the user is trying to do
template.description: What is wrong in the current experience

evidence.observed_where: URL, Figma frame, screenshot reference or screen name
evidence.expected_behaviour: What the user would reasonably expect

template.user_impact: Why this causes friction, confusion, mistrust, delay or error
template.recommendation: Suggested improvement written as a direction, not an over-prescribed final solution
template.owner: Design | Product | Engineering | Content | Research | Unknown
template.status: new | triaged | in_progress | fixed | accepted_risk | needs_research

scale.label: not_a_problem
scale.definition: Not a usability issue or not enough evidence to include.

scale.label: low
scale.definition: Minor friction, polish issue or small clarity problem. Users can still complete the task.

scale.label: medium
scale.definition: Noticeable friction. Some users may slow down, misunderstand, need help or make a recoverable mistake.

scale.label: high
scale.definition: Serious issue. Users may fail the task, lose confidence, create incorrect data or need support.

scale.label: critical
scale.definition: Blocking or high-risk issue. Users cannot complete a key task, or the issue creates serious legal, financial, safety, privacy or operational risk.

scoring_inputs.name: impact
scoring_inputs.question: How badly does this affect the user’s ability to complete the task?

scoring_inputs.name: frequency
scoring_inputs.question: How often are users likely to encounter it?

scoring_inputs.name: persistence
scoring_inputs.question: Can users recover easily, or does the issue keep following them around like a tiny UX gremlin?

scoring_inputs.name: risk
scoring_inputs.question: Could this cause serious data, trust, compliance, financial or safety consequences?

scoring_inputs.name: confidence
scoring_inputs.question: How confident are we that this is a real issue?

severity_rules: Use critical when a user is blocked from a core task or when the mistake could create serious legal, financial, privacy, safety or compliance risk.
Use high when the task can technically continue but users are likely to fail, abandon, create incorrect data or need support.
Use medium when the issue creates confusion, hesitation, avoidable effort or recoverable mistakes.
Use low when the issue is mostly polish, small inconsistency or minor inefficiency.
If confidence is low, either mark the finding as needs_research or reduce priority until validated.
Do not raise severity just because a stakeholder dislikes something.
Do not lower severity just because the fix is difficult.

contents: Number of critical, high, medium and low findings

good_report_traits: Specific enough for designers and developers
Not overloaded with every tiny preference
Includes what not to fix yet

before_review: Are user goals and tasks listed?
Are all evaluators using the same heuristic set?
Are screenshots or references easy to capture?
during_review: Is each finding tied to a user task?
Is each finding mapped to a primary heuristic?
Is the observed evidence separate from the recommendation?
Is severity based on impact rather than opinion?
Are accessibility issues being captured properly?
before_sharing_report: Can a non-UX stakeholder understand the top issues?
Can a designer act on the recommendations?
Can a developer identify where the issue occurs?
Are critical and high issues clearly justified?
Are research gaps separated from confirmed findings?
Are quick wins and bigger strategic fixes separated?
Is the report short enough to be read?

anti_patterns.name: The opinion parade
anti_patterns.description: The evaluation becomes a list of personal design preferences.
anti_patterns.how_to_avoid: Tie every finding to a user goal, heuristic and observed evidence.

anti_patterns.name: The screenshot graveyard
anti_patterns.description: The report contains many screenshots but does not explain impact or priority.
anti_patterns.how_to_avoid: Every screenshot must support a clear issue, user impact and recommendation.

anti_patterns.name: The severity soup
anti_patterns.description: Everything is marked high, so nothing is actually prioritised.
anti_patterns.how_to_avoid: Use the severity model and reserve critical/high for task failure, high risk or major friction.

anti_patterns.name: The accessibility afterthought
anti_patterns.description: Accessibility is reviewed only after visual and interaction issues.
anti_patterns.how_to_avoid: Include accessibility questions in the core evaluation pass.

anti_patterns.name: The solution cannon
anti_patterns.description: Evaluators jump straight to detailed redesigns before agreeing what the problem is.
anti_patterns.how_to_avoid: Write the problem first, then a recommendation direction.

anti_patterns.name: The lonely evaluator
anti_patterns.description: One person reviews everything and blind spots sneak through wearing tiny slippers.
anti_patterns.how_to_avoid: Use at least two evaluators when possible and calibrate severity together.

example_finding.title: Users may not understand what action to take from the dashboard warning
example_finding.user_task: Identify where to go to fix unmatched or unattached units
example_finding.description: The warning highlights that a coverage issue exists, but the next action is not clear enough. Users may understand that something is wrong without knowing where to go or what fixing it involves.

evidence.observed_behaviour: The warning takes prominent dashboard space but does not clearly explain the fix path.
evidence.expected_behaviour: The warning should act as a signpost, showing what is wrong, why it matters and where to go next.

example_finding.user_impact: Users may treat the metric as stagnant information rather than an actionable route to improve coverage.
example_finding.recommendation: Make the warning more action-oriented by adding a clear next step, such as 'Review unmatched units', and explain the impact of fixing the issue.
